\chapter{What the Body Feels --- Chest, Strength, Rest, Fear, Laughter}
\label{ch:fuerza-y-risa}
\hlchaptermodality{315}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the chest, and say strength, rest, fear and laughter in Spanish.}

Complete ES-C315-risa: name all five, and say which two of them are opposites.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el pecho]{el pecho — the chest you can run backwards}

\label{lesson:ES-C315-pecho}



\begin{quote}
What is an \emph{audience}, literally? (A hearing.) And what flower is a lion's tooth? (The dandelion.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la noche — took the same road out of Latin.
  \item la espalda — the other side of this one.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{PE-cho}, two beats. The \emph{ch} is the \emph{ch} of English \emph{church}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el pecho} — \textquotedblleft{}the chest.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{pectus}. The thing to watch is the middle of it: a Latin \emph{ct} comes out as a Spanish \emph{ch}, and it does so with almost no exceptions.

You have already met the result without being handed the rule. Latin \emph{noctem} is \emph{la noche}. Latin \emph{octo} is \emph{ocho}. Latin \emph{factum} is \emph{hecho}. Latin \emph{lactem} is \emph{leche}. And Latin \emph{pectus} is \emph{el pecho}.

So when a Spanish word has \emph{ch} in the middle, there is usually a Latin \emph{ct} underneath it — and usually an English word sitting on that \emph{ct}: \emph{nocturnal}, \emph{octave}, \emph{fact}, \emph{lactose}, \textbf{pectoral}.

The strangest survivor is medical. To \textbf{expectorate} is to cough something up: \emph{ex-pectore}, \textquotedblleft{}out of the chest.\textquotedblright{} It is a very long word for a very short act, and it is built on this one.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The chest, and a rule you can run in either direction.

\emph{Ch} in the middle of a Spanish word, \emph{ct} in the Latin behind it, and an English word usually waiting on the far side.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el pecho}
  \item \emph{el pecho y la espalda}
  \item \emph{el oído}, then \emph{el pecho}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does Latin \emph{ct} become in Spanish? (\emph{Ch}.) Which word for a time of day proves it? (\emph{La noche}, from \emph{noctem}.) And what does \emph{expectorate} mean, taken apart? (Out of the chest.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la fuerza]{la fuerza — the strength inside comfort}

\label{lesson:ES-C315-fuerza}



\begin{quote}
What does Latin \emph{ct} turn into? (\emph{Ch}.) And what is an \emph{audition}? (A hearing.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el sueño — its \emph{o} broke the same way.
  \item enfermo — the state where this runs short.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{FUER-za}, two beats. One slide through the middle, not two vowels. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la fuerza} — \textquotedblleft{}the strength,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the force.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{fortis} meant strong. Its abstract noun \textbf{fortia} meant strength. Spanish broke the stressed \emph{o} into \emph{ue}, exactly as \emph{somnus} became \emph{el sueño}: \emph{fortia} becomes \emph{fuerza}.

That is the other crack, and now you have both of them.

A stressed \emph{e} goes to \emph{ie}: \emph{piel}, \emph{pierna}, \emph{pie}, \emph{diente}. A stressed \emph{o} goes to \emph{ue}: \emph{sueño}, \emph{fuerza}. Two vowels, two breaks, and between them they account for a very large share of the Spanish dictionary.

English has \emph{fortis} lying in the open. A \textbf{fort} is a strong place. To \textbf{fortify} is to make strong. \textbf{Force} is \emph{fortia} itself, arrived through French. An \textbf{effort} is strength put \emph{out}.

And then \textbf{comfort}. It is \emph{com-fortare}: to strengthen thoroughly. To comfort somebody was not originally to soothe them — it was to put strength into them. The soft modern sense is a late arrival, and \emph{la fuerza} is the word still sitting underneath it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Both cracks, fully stated.

\emph{E} breaks to \emph{ie}. \emph{O} breaks to \emph{ue}. Every word in these two chapters that could take one has taken it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la fuerza}
  \item \emph{no tengo fuerza}
  \item \emph{el pecho}, then \emph{la fuerza}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{fortis} mean? (Strong.) What is \emph{comfort}, taken apart? (To strengthen thoroughly.) And which break turned \emph{fortia} into \emph{fuerza}? (\emph{O} to \emph{ue}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el descanso]{el descanso — the undoing of tiredness}

\label{lesson:ES-C315-descanso}



\begin{quote}
What is \emph{comfort} built on? (\emph{Fortis} — strong.) And what does a Spanish \emph{ch} usually sit on in Latin? (A \emph{ct}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la fuerza — what this gives back.
  \item el sueño — a deeper version of the same thing.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{des-CAN-so}, three beats, stress in the middle. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el descanso} — \textquotedblleft{}the rest,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the break.\textquotedblright{}

This one is assembled in front of you. \emph{Cansar} is \textquotedblleft{}to tire.\textquotedblright{} \emph{Des-} undoes a verb. \emph{Descansar} is \textquotedblleft{}to un-tire,\textquotedblright{} and \emph{el descanso} is the noun: the pause in which the un-tiring happens.

Spanish does not name rest as a thing in its own right. It names it by what it reverses. Rest is the taking-back-off of tiredness.

\emph{Cansar} has a stranger history than it looks. It is Latin \textbf{campsare}, \textquotedblleft{}to turn about, to double back\textquotedblright{} — a sailor's word for rounding a headland — and Latin had it from Greek \textbf{kamptein}, to bend. A ship that had rounded the cape had done the hard part of the voyage. From \textquotedblleft{}turned the corner\textquotedblright{} to \textquotedblleft{}worn out by turning it\textquotedblright{} is a short walk, and Spanish walked it.

English has no everyday descendant of \emph{kamptein}, so there is no cognate to collect here. What there is instead is the seam. \emph{Des-} is the same prefix as English \textbf{dis-}, so \emph{descanso} is built exactly like \emph{disarm}, \emph{disband} and \emph{dislodge}: a verb with its work run backwards.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A word you could have assembled yourself.

\emph{Des-} is English \emph{dis-}. Once you can see that seam, a large family of Spanish verbs comes apart in your hands.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el descanso}
  \item \emph{un descanso, por favor}
  \item \emph{la fuerza}, then \emph{el descanso}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{des-} do to a verb? (Undoes it.) What is \emph{cansar}? (To tire.) And what was \emph{campsare}, at sea? (To round a headland.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el miedo]{el miedo — the fear inside meticulous}

\label{lesson:ES-C315-miedo}



\begin{quote}
What does \emph{des-} do? (Undoes the verb.) And what is an \emph{effort}? (Strength put out.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item tranquilo — its opposite.
  \item triste — its neighbour.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{MIE-do}, two beats. The \emph{d} between vowels is soft, close to the \emph{th} of \emph{this}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el miedo} — \textquotedblleft{}the fear.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{metus}, and the \emph{e} breaks to \emph{ie} once more. That is the fifth time. By now you should expect it before you are told.

English has one descendant of \emph{metus} and it is well hidden: \textbf{meticulous}. It is \emph{metus} plus \emph{-culosus}, \textquotedblleft{}full of fear.\textquotedblright{} A meticulous person was, in Latin, a frightened one — somebody so afraid of getting it wrong that they checked everything twice, and then checked it again.

English kept the checking and let the fear go. \emph{Meticulous} is now a compliment. But the dread is still down in the word, and \emph{el miedo} is the part that got left behind.

It sits neatly among what you already have. \emph{Tranquilo} is its opposite. \emph{Triste} is its neighbour.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The fifth \emph{ie}, and the darker half of this chapter.

One more feeling closes it out — and it is the opposite of this one.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el miedo}
  \item \emph{tengo miedo}
  \item \emph{el descanso}, then \emph{el miedo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{meticulous} mean in Latin? (Full of fear.) What is the Latin behind \emph{miedo}? (\emph{Metus}.) And which of your five answers is its opposite? (\emph{Tranquilo}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la risa]{la risa — the laugh under ridicule}

\label{lesson:ES-C315-risa}



\begin{quote}
What is \emph{meticulous}, in Latin? (Full of fear.) And what does \emph{des-} do to \emph{cansar}? (Undoes the tiring.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item contento — the state this comes out of.
  \item el miedo — what it is furthest from.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{RI-sa}, two beats. An \emph{r} at the start of a word is rolled, not tapped. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la risa} — \textquotedblleft{}the laughter.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{ridere} was \textquotedblleft{}to laugh,\textquotedblright{} and \textbf{risus} was the laugh itself. Spanish kept both halves cleanly: \emph{reír} to laugh, \emph{la risa} the laughter.

English took the root, and took it badly. Every descendant it kept is unkind. To \textbf{ridicule} somebody is to laugh at them. To \textbf{deride} is \emph{de-ridere}, to laugh \emph{down} at them. \textbf{Derision} is the noun for doing it. \textbf{Risible} means laughable, and it has never once been a compliment.

So English has four words from \emph{ridere} and not one of them is a happy laugh. Spanish has \emph{la risa}, which is the ordinary, warm, unloaded word — the sound a room makes when something is funny.

That is worth noticing about borrowing generally. A language rarely takes a whole word. It takes one \emph{use} of the word, and the use it takes is very often the sharp one.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Ten of the body and what it feels.

And a hinge. The next chapter opens on the other side of this word — what the face does when the laughing stops.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la risa}
  \item \emph{la risa y el miedo}
  \item \emph{el pecho, la fuerza, el descanso, el miedo, la risa}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \emph{risus}? (The laugh.) Name an English word from \emph{ridere}. (\emph{Ridicule}, \emph{deride}, \emph{derision} or \emph{risible}.) And what do all of them have in common? (Not one is kind.)
\end{tcolorbox}
